name: American Arts and Crafts

geography.hearth: Boston and Chicago as intellectual centres; Stickley's workshops at Eastwood, New York, as the transmission point

lineage.note: Ruskin and Morris arrive as text and as furniture before they arrive as buildings. The Boston Society of Arts and Crafts (1897), Elbert Hubbard's Roycroft (1895) and Gustav Stickley's United Crafts (1898) are all deliberate transplants of an English reform programme.
The American formal substrate: the continuous unornamented skin, the open living hall organized on a hearth, and the horizontal spread of the plan are inherited directly, not imported.
Richardson's insistence that material be shown doing its work, and his base-shaft-cap masonry hierarchy, pass into the movement through the Shingle Style and through Sullivan's office.
The specific target is machine-sawn applied ornament sold by the linear foot from a millwork catalog. The reform is not anti-decoration; it is a demand that decoration be produced by construction.

description.short: The American branch of the Arts and Crafts reform, which held that ornament must arise from construction and that a house, its furniture, and its site are a single commission, and which reorganized the middle-class plan around an open hearth-centred living room.
description.long:
American Arts and Crafts is a reform movement before it is a style, and this matters for how the node behaves in a graph: its defining content is a rule about where ornament may come from. Ornament must be produced by the act of building — by the joint, the bracket, the rafter end, the change of material at a structural transition — and not applied to a surface after the fact. Everything the movement looks like follows from that rule. Wood is left unpainted or matte-stained so that the grain and the joinery remain legible. Porch supports are battered piers on heavy bases because that is what a compressive member honestly looks like. Windows group into bands because they are openings between structural posts rather than punched holes in a decorated wall. The movement's American originality lies in its scale: where William Morris built for wealthy patrons, Stickley, Hubbard, and the Chicago and Pasadena architects built for a salaried professional class, and then published the result.

The conditions that produced it are specific and largely economic. The scroll saw, the moulding machine, and the national millwork catalog had, by the 1880s, made ornament cheaper than plainness, and the visible result was a generation of houses wearing decoration that no one had made and no one could account for. The Panic of 1893 discredited the display culture attached to it. At the same moment the domestic servant supply collapsed for middle-class households, which quietly rewrote the plan: the formal parlour, the back stair, and the segregated dining room became liabilities, and the open living room with built-in cabinetry, a hearth, and a plate rail became the answer — fewer rooms, fewer surfaces to dust, fewer pieces of furniture to move. The mail-order catalog and the mass magazine, the very instruments of the ornament glut, then became the movement's own distribution system. Stickley's The Craftsman (1901-1916) is the pivotal case: a magazine that printed Morris and Ruskin alongside measured plans a local carpenter could execute, which is to say a magazine that converted an ideology into a buildable specification.

What it reacts against is therefore not the Victorian era in general but a particular industrial dishonesty: the imitation of handwork by machine. The movement's American compromise, and it is an intelligent one, is to accept the machine where the machine does honest work — dimensional lumber, plate glass, cast hardware — and to reserve the hand for the joint and the finish. Greene and Greene push this to its limit in Pasadena, where the pegged scarf joints and rounded timber ends of the Gamble House are simultaneously a display of craft and a demonstration of how a stick of wood terminates. Stickley pushes it in the opposite direction, toward reproducibility, and it is Stickley's direction that produces a national vernacular.

To stand in one of these rooms is to be in a space that is lower and darker than a Victorian room and considerably calmer. The ceiling is beamed and near, often eight and a half feet. Light arrives filtered through art glass in rectilinear geometry and does not glare. The wood is brown and matte and absorbs rather than reflects. The hearth is the largest object in the room and everything is arranged with reference to it, including built-in seating that cannot be moved, which is the movement's most radical and least remarked act: the plan is fixed against redecoration. Outside, the eaves are wide enough that the wall is in shadow for most of the day, and the shadow is what gives a plain wall its interest. This last point is the one the twentieth century will spend the next fifty years forgetting.

defining_characteristics: Ornament produced by construction — exposed joinery, rafter tails, purlins, brackets, and material transitions — rather than applied to a finished surface
The hearth as the generative centre of the plan, with an open living room replacing the parlour and built-in cabinetry replacing movable furniture
Materials left in their own colour and texture: unpainted or matte-stained wood, clinker brick, river rock, stucco, matte tile
Horizontal emphasis established by low broad roofs, wide eaves, and continuous window and trim bands
House, interior fittings, furniture, and garden conceived as one commission under one grammar
Absence of applied classical orders and of machine-sawn Victorian ornament
diagnostic_tells: Exposed rafter tails and knee braces that continue the actual framing rather than being screwed on
Battered (tapered) porch piers standing on heavy masonry bases at least two feet wide
Wide flat unpainted trim, a plate rail at door head height, and bookcases built into the wall flanking the fireplace
Art glass in rectilinear, non-floral geometry, usually confined to upper sash and cabinet doors
Two or three natural materials stacked base-to-top on one elevation (stone base, shingle middle, stucco gable) with each change occurring at a structural line

distinguished_from.difference: Queen Anne ornament is sawn, turned, and applied to the surface; Arts and Crafts ornament is the structure itself left visible. If a bracket would fall off without changing anything, it is Queen Anne.
Colonial Revival restores bilateral symmetry, applied classical orders, and painted trim — all three of which American Arts and Crafts explicitly rejects.

Prairie abstracts and suppresses structural evidence into continuous planes; Arts and Crafts insists on displaying it. A clean soffit with no visible rafter is Prairie; a rafter tail is Arts and Crafts.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No canonical module. Proportion is set by two datums and one structural rhythm: the horizontal line of the porch beam, the aligned head height of all doors and windows, and the spacing of the stud or timber bay that the exposed members declare. The system is dimensional rather than ratio-based, which is why it scales badly upward — an Arts and Crafts house of more than two storeys loses its logic.
typical_ratios: Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 inches
Wall plate 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 0 in at the principal floor
Window and door heads aligned at a single datum, 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft 0 in above finish floor
Porch depth 7 to 9 ft — deep enough to furnish
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Windows grouped into ribbons of two to four units between structural posts rather than isolated as punched openings; the group, not the sash, is the compositional unit.

massing_affinities.note: The single-storey hearth-centred bungalow is the movement's most-built vessel.
The 'Craftsman foursquare' — the movement's grammar applied to an efficient two-storey urban box on a narrow lot.
Shared with the Prairie branch; the pinwheel plan is common ancestry, not a distinguishing trait.

constraints.statement: Exposed rafter tails must correspond to actual rafters at 16 to 24 in on centre and project 24 to 36 in beyond the wall plane. Decorative tails applied to a boxed eave are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the projection beyond the wall plane. The 16-24in on-centre rafter spacing has no vocabulary variable (rafter spacing is not named) and stays prose, as does the prohibition on decorative (non-structural) tails.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch between 4:12 and 6:12. Pitches above 8:12 belong to the Tudor and Storybook families and break the horizontal reading.

Applied classical orders — fluted or turned columns, pedimented door surrounds, dentil courses — are forbidden. Porch supports must be square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide.

test.note: Tests the masonry base width. The prohibition on applied classical orders (columns, pedimented surrounds, dentil courses) is a categorical list with no vocabulary variable enumerating forbidden ornament and stays prose.

constraints.statement: All window and door heads on a given storey align to one datum, tolerance zero. Transoms and clerestories may sit above that datum only where the wall plate is raised for the whole bay.

test.note: Tests the zero-tolerance datum rule. The transom/clerestory exception (permitted above the datum only where the wall plate is raised for the whole bay) stays prose.

constraints.statement: No more than three wall materials per elevation, each change occurring at a structural line (water table, belt, plate) and returning fully around any corner it meets.

test.note: Tests the material-count ceiling. Where changes must occur (a structural line) and the corner-return requirement stay prose.

exemplars.name: Gamble House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene. The movement's high-craft limit case: every joint, hardware piece, rug, and light fitting designed under one commission.
exemplars.why: The building the movement is known by, and the one HABS chose to record: its survey's own significance line calls it 'one of the finest examples of the American Craftsman Movement'. SAH Archipedia, writing about the Riordan Mansion, says the Gamble House 'is considered the epitome of Arts and Crafts architecture in America' -- that sentence is on the riordan-mansion record, not on this one, which is where a reader must go to check it.

exemplars.name: Craftsman Farms (the Log House)
exemplars.note: Gustav Stickley's own house, built 1908-1911. The theorist of The Craftsman building for himself in chestnut logs and fieldstone.
exemplars.why: The theorist's own house, and therefore the type specimen for the reproducible half of the movement rather than the high-craft half -- the judgment is the National Register's, which lists it, and the node's own reading of Stickley against Greene and Greene.

exemplars.name: Roycroft Campus
exemplars.note: Elbert Hubbard's craft colony, built out c. 1897-1915. The American attempt at a Morris-style guild settlement, and the commercial engine that sold the idea nationally.
exemplars.why: The type specimen for the movement as a GUILD rather than as a house, on the Roycroft Campus Corporation's own claim that it 'is the best preserved and most complete complex of buildings remaining in the United States of the "guilds"' and on the National Historic Landmark district designation of 1986.

exemplars.name: Robert R. Blacker House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene, 1907. The other Pasadena ultimate bungalow, larger than the Gamble House and a year earlier; carried because a movement should not be represented by one commission from one office.
exemplars.why: A documented Greene and Greene house of the same office and a year earlier than the Gamble House -- the record gives 1907 against 1908-1909 -- listed on the National Register, and therefore the control against which the Gamble House's singularity can be read; the judgment is this project's, and the record notes that no HABS survey of it was found.

exemplars.name: Riordan Mansion
exemplars.note: Charles Whittlesey, 1904. A duplex of two near-mirror houses for two brothers in a territorial logging town, in log slab, volcanic stone and hand-split shake -- the movement working in the materials its owners milled themselves, four years before the Gamble House.
exemplars.why: The Society of Architectural Historians' own entry calls it 'among the best examples of Craftsman architecture in Arizona' and notes that it 'predates by four years' the Gamble House, which makes it the movement's Southwestern expression rather than a specimen of its Pasadena hearth.

exemplars.name: Marston House
exemplars.note: Hebbard and Gill, designed 1904 and built 1905. A large Arts and Crafts house rather than a bungalow, by the partnership Irving Gill would shortly leave in the opposite direction; the movement at its most Southern Californian and least Pasadena.
exemplars.why: The National Trust for Historic Preservation calls it 'One of California's finest examples of the Arts and Crafts movement', and it is carried as the San Diego expression rather than a type specimen because its architects' later work runs away from this node.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Wendy Kaplan (ed.), 'The Art That Is Life': The Arts and Crafts Movement in America, 1875-1920 (1987)
Alan Gowans, The Comfortable House: North American Suburban Architecture 1890-1930 (1986)
Edward R. Bosley, Greene and Greene (2000)

proportion_packs.note: States the system in almost the same words as craftsman -- 'two datums and one structural rhythm' -- and adds the sentence that gives the grouping rule its point: 'the group, not the sash, is the compositional unit.' It also supplies the one qualification the pack quotes verbatim in its porch rule, that the porch is 'deep enough to furnish', which is a functional dimension rather than a compositional one and is the honest reason a porch of this type is seven feet and not five.

The movement's own governing rule -- ornament must be produced by construction, never applied after the fact -- is this pack's whole argument restated from the furniture side: 'there is no pedestal, no column and no entablature... the module is a board... the room does not generate the trim; the lumber yard does.' Bound as the interior counterpart to the node's own hard constraint (c03) forbidding applied classical orders. The pack's own applies_to list names this node directly, and its sources -- Stickley's Craftsman magazine among them -- are the movement's own transmission mechanism, not an analogous system borrowed from elsewhere.

Governs the 'balanced-asymmetrical' composition the node's own proportional_system describes only qualitatively (two datums and a structural rhythm, 'dimensional rather than ratio-based'): this pack's window_grouping_rule (openings gathered in groups of two to four between structural posts, adjacent groups differing in count) is precisely the node's own diagnostic that windows 'group into ribbons... the group, not the sash, is the compositional unit,' and its continuous-datum rule (water table and head line unbroken through every mass) is what makes the node's stacked base-shingle-stucco material hierarchy -- a defining characteristic -- read as one wall rather than three. Not given the top role: the movement genuinely has no module of its own at this level of generality, which the node's own proportional_system says outright, so no pack here stands in as an order-equivalent 'primary.'

declined_packs.reason: A Chambers Ionic order as this node's PRIMARY proportioning system. The node's own record refuses the classical order outright, so the pack arrives to dimension a column, entablature and pilaster the style does not have.

declined_packs.note: Delivered by english-georgian at cascade depth 5-6 with no direct lineage edge between the two -- which is why this is written on the node and not on an edge.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes describe an order skeleton quoted from Ware — column at 9 modules, entablature a fifth of it divided 4 : 3 : 5, a modillion cornice, an Attic base — and it dimensions column, entablature, cornice, crown and porch_support here. The node carries a HARD constraint forbidding applied classical orders by name, and the same constraint then states what a porch support must be instead: square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide. That is the pack's subject contradicted at its own address, not a blanket refusal: the node is not silent about orders, it enumerates the members and prohibits them. The node has already written this exact refusal against chambers-ionic; palladio-ionic is the same object arriving from english-palladian at depth 8 instead.
declined_packs.quote: Applied classical orders — fluted or turned columns, pedimented door surrounds, dentil courses — are forbidden
declined_packs.note: Governs 1 slot: frieze. Declining passes frieze to palladio-tuscan (italian-renaissance); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. Worth stating plainly: the decline stops THIS order and does not stop the classical order as such — the fallback is another classical pack, which is OQ 58's stated limit one layer down.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's module note says that deciding whether a gable is the end of a roof, a parapet carried up past the roof plane, or a screen standing clear of it "is prior to any dimension in this pack", and every rule under it is a masonry gable treatment: apex at 0.72 of the base, coping stones, crow-step tread and rise, kneelers, screen-gable facade ratios. The node's hard c02 caps the principal pitch at 4:12 to 6:12, which puts the apex of a roof-end gable at 0.17 to 0.25 of its width against the pack's 0.72, and the quoted sentence names the families the taller triangle belongs to and says why this style cannot have it. The node's own "Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 inches" settles the other two cases: a roof oversailing its gable wall by two to three feet is not a wall carried past the roof plane and capped, and a crow-step IS the verge treatment, which is why the pack's Scottish source records "no barge board". This is a mechanical contradiction in the node's own figures, not the blanket "no proportional system" sentence being stretched.
declined_packs.quote: Pitches above 8:12 belong to the Tudor and Storybook families and break the horizontal reading

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own overlay note says what it is about: a module of sixty minutes, a column at 7 modules with a quarter diminution, a half-diameter base and capital with their internal divisions, and a plain 1-module pedestal — "enough to lay out the column and the pedestal completely." It dimensions column, entablature and porch_support here. The node carries a HARD constraint that forbids applied classical orders by enumerating their members, and then states positively what a porch support must be instead: a square post or a battered pier on a masonry base of at least 24 in. That is the pack's subject contradicted at its own address by figures the node states about itself, not the blanket "no canonical module" sentence being stretched — and the node has already written this same refusal twice, against chambers-ionic and palladio-ionic, which are the same object arriving down other branches.
declined_packs.quote: Applied classical orders — fluted or turned columns, pedimented door surrounds, dentil courses — are forbidden. Porch supports must be square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide.

Declining passes frieze to vignola-tuscan (roman-classical) and steps_and_stoop to facade-peristyle (english-palladian); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. As with palladio-ionic, the decline stops THIS order and not the classical order as such — both fallbacks are themselves classical packs, OQ 58's stated limit one layer down.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes describe four deltas to a Doric ORDER — an Attic base after Palladio, a single-fascia architrave with conical drops after the Theatre of Marcellus, a pedestal at three tenths divided 2 : 6 : 1, and a diminution by Blondel's conchoid — plus the module's thirtieths and a column-height band. Its declared slots are column, pilaster, crown, frieze, modillion_dentil and porch_support. The node's hard c03 forbids applied classical orders and names two of those members outright (turned columns, dentil courses), and its defining_characteristics repeat the refusal as "Absence of applied classical orders and of machine-sawn Victorian ornament." The contradiction is between the pack's stated subject and the node's own enumerated prohibition, not a category-versus-authority quibble: the node is not silent about orders, it lists the parts and bans them.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own note states its subject as the order where Palladio and Vignola part -- a column of nine and a half diameters bound to a two-diameter intercolumniation -- and it dimensions chair_rail, column, crown, entablature, height_proportion, modillion_dentil and porch_support on this node. The node carries a HARD constraint that forbids applied classical orders by enumerating their members, dentil courses among them, and then states positively what a porch support must be instead: a square post or a battered pier on a masonry base not less than 24 in wide. Three of the pack's seven addresses are answered by that one sentence, and the node's governing_logic adds that its system 'is dimensional rather than ratio-based', which is the precise opposite of an order laid out in modules and parts. This is the fifth order pack refused here on the same constraint, after chambers-ionic, palladio-ionic, palladio-tuscan and chambers-doric.

declined_packs.reason: Tuscan encoded from Vignola's own figures in modules and parts, dimensioning balustrade, baseboard, casing, chair_rail, cornice, crown, door_surround, entablature, frieze, porch_depth and porch_support. Two of those addresses are answered by name in the node's hard constraint -- 'pedimented door surrounds ... are forbidden' meets door_surround, and 'Porch supports must be square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide' meets porch_support -- so this is the pack's own subject contradicted at its own addresses. It does NOT reach porch_depth: that rule is a flat 96 in flagged a judgment slot, whose own note says the order 'cannot fix the depth for you'. Two addresses, not three rather than the 'no canonical module' sentence being stretched. The plainness of the Tuscan is not a defence: the constraint forbids the applied order, not the enriched one. Sixth order pack refused here on the same constraint.

Stated plainly because the direction is uncomfortable and the chain is now visible: this node's earlier palladio-tuscan decline passed frieze TO vignola-tuscan, and this decline passes it on again to a RICHER order than the one refused. The decline stops this order and not the classical order as such -- OQ 58's stated limit, one layer down. The node's frieze wants trim-craftsman, which it already binds; supplying that is a binding decision, not a decline.
